lesson.title: The Trig Integral Family: Six Rules Built by Working Derivatives Backward
lesson.summary: Every basic trigonometric derivative you already know has a mirror image integral. This chapter previews all six pairs and shows the reverse engineering trick that generates every one of them.
lesson.body:
By this point you know six basic trigonometric derivative rules: the derivative of sin(x) is cos(x), the derivative of cos(x) is -sin(x), the derivative of tan(x) is sec^2(x), the derivative of cot(x) is -csc^2(x), the derivative of sec(x) is sec(x)*tan(x), and the derivative of csc(x) is -csc(x)*cot(x). Every one of those six facts has a partner integral fact hiding inside it, because integration is defined as the reverse process of differentiation.

The trick is simple to state: if you already know that the derivative of some function G(x) is F(x), then you automatically know that the integral of F(x) dx is G(x) + C. You do not need a separate proof or a new formula, you just read the derivative equation from right to left. This single idea, reverse engineering a known derivative, is the entire method behind every trig integral rule you will meet in this unit.

Applying that trick to all six derivative facts above produces the six basic trig integral rules: integral of sin(x) dx = -cos(x) + C, integral of cos(x) dx = sin(x) + C, integral of sec^2(x) dx = tan(x) + C, integral of csc^2(x) dx = -cot(x) + C, integral of sec(x)*tan(x) dx = sec(x) + C, and integral of csc(x)*cot(x) dx = -csc(x) + C. Each of these gets its own focused chapter next, where you will see the reasoning worked out in full and practice recognizing the pattern.

Notice the direct connection to the derivative of sine, listed as a building block for this chapter. Since the derivative of sin(x) is cos(x), reading that backward tells you immediately that integral of cos(x) dx = sin(x) + C, no extra work required. That one step is a template for how every rule in this family gets built: start from a memorized derivative, then flip the statement around.

Here is a small worked example that combines this idea with the constant multiple rule from the previous chapter. Find integral of 3*cos(x) dx. Pull the constant out: 3 * integral of cos(x) dx. Since integral of cos(x) dx = sin(x) + C, the result is 3*sin(x) + C. Check by differentiating: the derivative of 3*sin(x) is 3*cos(x), which matches the original integrand.

A useful habit going forward: rather than memorizing six integral formulas as isolated facts, memorize the six derivative pairs you already learned and treat each integral as simply that pair read backward. This keeps the rules connected to something you understand, instead of six more things to forget.
